explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. God says He will “…cut off its supply of food…” and send famine on the land. Picture a bakery with a warm oven and no flour. That's just a room with a sad apron in it. Food is the first thing on His list.

Water is a good guess, friend, but this verse never mentions it. God says He will stretch out His hand against the land to cut off its supply of food. After that He mentions famine and cutting off man and beast. Food comes first, and the rivers and wells never come up.

Trade sounds sensible, but it isn't in the verse. God never brings up other nations here. He says He will cut off the land's supply of food and send famine upon it. So the answer is food, and that's the one thing on the table.

Yes, baker. God says He will cut off food, send famine, and cut off “…both man and beast…” That's the whole land feeling it, people and animals together. Notice He puts it as a what-if about an unfaithful land.

This one is true, friend, so it didn't land where you hoped. God says He will cut off the land's supply of food and send famine. He also says He will cut off from it “…both man and beast…” The people and the animals are both named in that verse.

Right on the money, baker. God says that even with those three men in the land, “…their righteousness could deliver only themselves…” (Ezekiel 14:14). It's a full-size ALL-STAR righteousness, and it still covers just the three of them. That's a heavy line, so I think it's worth reading slowly.

You'd think the land would get a break with those three in it, wouldn't you? But the verse says their righteousness could deliver only themselves (Ezekiel 14:14). The land isn't on that list. Later, in the wild beasts what-if, God says “…the land would be desolate.” (Ezekiel 14:16).

That's a kind thought, friend, but the verse draws the line tighter. God says their righteousness could deliver only themselves. No friends are added to the list. It's a short list, and it's just those three men.

I get the thought, baker, because a parent's heart goes there first. But God says the opposite: “…even if these three men were in it, they could not deliver their own sons or daughters.” (Ezekiel 14:16) The text says they alone would be delivered. So this statement is false.

You caught it, friend. God says even those three men “…could not deliver their own sons or daughters.” They alone would be delivered, but the land would be desolate (Ezekiel 14:16). Even with those three men there, nobody else is on the list.

That's the one, baker. God says, “Or if I send a plague into that land and pour out My wrath upon it through bloodshed…” That makes four what-ifs: famine, wild beasts, sword and plague. Same three men, same answer.

Water's a fair guess, friend, but a flood isn't in this list. In the fourth what-if, God says He will send a plague into that land. The four things in this passage are famine, wild beasts, a sword and a plague. A flood never makes the cut.

Hail is a dramatic guess, baker, but it's not in this passage. God says He will send a plague into the land and pour out His wrath through bloodshed. Hail never shows up in the verse. The fourth thing on the list is a plague.

Yes, baker! God says, “How much worse will it be when I send against Jerusalem My four dire judgments…” The what-ifs about a land in general end, and He names a real city. The talk gets personal right there.
Babylon is a fair guess, friend, but God doesn't name it here. He says He will send His four dire judgments against Jerusalem. After the what-if lands, He points straight at that city.

Nineveh is a big name in the Bible, baker. It's the city Jonah, a prophet, was sent to (Jonah 1:2). But this passage never names it. When God turns from the what-if lands to a real city, the city is Jerusalem.
Four it is, baker. God says, “…My four dire judgments—sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague…” You just walked through each one as a what-if. Now He says all four are coming against Jerusalem.

Three is the number of men in the story, friend, so I see how it crept in. But God says He is sending four dire judgments. They are sword, famine, wild beasts and plague. Those are the four what-ifs you just walked through.

Seven is a big, famous number, baker, but it's not in this verse. God names four dire judgments: sword, famine, wild beasts and plague. Those are the same four you met in the what-ifs. No extra ones are added.

That sounds like the end of the story, baker, but God keeps going. He says, “Yet, behold, some survivors will be left in it—sons and daughters who will be brought out.” So people do come out of Jerusalem. The statement is false.

You caught the turn, friend. God says, “Yet, behold, some survivors will be left in it—sons and daughters who will be brought out.” Then He says “They will come out to you, and when you see their conduct and actions, you will be comforted…” (Ezekiel 14:22). The statement is false because survivors are named.

Comfort, baker. God says, “…you will be comforted regarding the disaster I have brought upon Jerusalem…” Then in verse 23 He says the survivors “…will bring you consolation…” That's a word of comfort after a heavy passage.
Shame isn't the word, friend, and I'm glad. God says the survivors' conduct and actions will bring comfort. In verse 23 He says they “…will bring you consolation…” So the word here is comfort.

Fear fits the mood, baker, with all those judgments flying around. But the verse points another way. God says that when you see the survivors' conduct and actions, “…you will be comforted regarding the disaster I have brought upon Jerusalem…” (Ezekiel 14:22). So the blank is comfort.

Yes, baker. God says, “…you will know that it was not without cause that I have done all these things within it…” Seeing the survivors' conduct and actions is what shows that. He says it to close out this whole passage.
The verse says the opposite, friend. God calls it what He has done: “…I have done all these things within it…” The point is that it was not without cause. So this answer pulls against the text.

explanations.answer: It was not as bad as feared
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but God never says it was milder than feared. He calls it a disaster He brought on Jerusalem. What the survivors' conduct and actions show is that it was “…not without cause…” So that's the answer.
